extracted.intended_audience: PR professionals and communications writers producing press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing the tone and voice of press releases so they read as neutral, factual, news-like communications rather than promotional marketing copy. Covers approach, distinctions between press/news releases, best practices, examples, and words/phrases to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core Principle: journalistic tone over promotional
rubrics_metrics.description: A journalistic tone that is neutral, factual, and news-like consistently outperforms an achievement tone that sounds overly excited or promotional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer neutral, factual, news-like wording rather than achievement or promotional language. This is the central organising principle for press release tone and voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: News/Factual Approach
rubrics_metrics.description: A press release should have a professional, journalistic tone that sounds like news rather than advertising: Neutral; Factual language; Objective presentation; Third person; Active voice; No editorializing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write like news copy: use third person and active voice, avoid editorializing, and present facts objectively. Aim for language that reads as reportorial rather than promotional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press release vs. News release distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Press release: Often dual purpose (inform + promote), more persuasive tone. News release: Purely informational, journalistic, neutral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice: write press releases like news releases (i.e., favor neutrality and journalistic presentation even if the release has promotional goals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practices for tone and voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended writing practices: Write in third person; Use active voice; Avoid jargon and buzzwords; Stay factual; Match tone to type of announcement; Let facts do the persuading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concise, reportorial sentences. Match the degree of persuasion to the announcement type but default to factual reporting. Avoid marketing-speak and rely on verifiable facts to persuade readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words to avoid (promotional red flags)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid superlatives and marketing buzzwords such as: 'Thrilled, excited, delighted, proud'; 'Game-changing, revolutionary, groundbreaking, unprecedented'; 'World-class, leading, premier, best-in-class'; 'Innovative, cutting-edge, state-of-the-art'; 'Robust, scalable, seamless'; 'Synergy, paradigm shift, leverage'; 'Solution' (especially with adjectives); Superlatives without proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These terms are flagged as overly promotional. If a claim is used, back it with evidence; otherwise remove subjective adjectives and superlatives. Watch for business jargon that signals marketing copy rather than news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit tone rubric / pass criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A press release passes the journalistic tone test if: Could be published as a news article with minimal edits; No first person ("we"); No marketing-speak; No subjective evaluative claims (unsupported); Quotes are conversational, not corporate; Neutral framing of news event; Subject of sentences = the news, not the company; Verbs are reportorial (announces, reports, releases) not promotional (transforms, revolutionizes, disrupts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist to evaluate tone: read the copy and ask whether it would need only minimal edits to become a news article. Replace first-person/company-centric subjects with the news event as subject; prefer reportorial verbs; ensure quotes sound like people speaking rather than corporate messaging. Example anti-pattern: 'We are absolutely thrilled... this revolutionary product will transform...' — rewrite to a neutral journalistic lead such as: 'TechCorp today announced the launch of SmartWidget Pro, a business automation tool designed to reduce manual data entry by streamlining workflow processes.'
